 From the Politics Desk Hakeem Jeffries’ progressive defectors reveal the limits of their power: From the Politics Desk
 Plus, preparing for a lengthy Trump-Congress showdown. Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 
 Jeffries says House Democrats will 'fight for an affordable America' 03:05 Get more news Live on Share Add NBC News to Google Nov. 18, 2026, 5:00 PM EST By The Politics Desk Welcome to From the Politics Desk , a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. 
 In today’s edition, Jonathan Allen digs into Hakeem Jeffries’ big win on Capitol Hill. Plus, Lawrence Hurley explains why President Donald Trump’s legal battles with Congress could stretch on long after he exits the White House. 
 — Adam Wollner 
 Hakeem Jeffries’ progressive defectors reveal the limits of their power 
 Analysis by Jonathan Allen
 Seven incoming members of the House Democratic Caucus made their first big move since winning their elections this month, publicly stating that they voted against Hakeem Jeffries ’ nomination to be the next speaker after a secret-ballot contest today. 
 Jeffries, who led his party to a historic rout of Republicans in November, faced no opponent. That made the fringe of his party, especially the progressive, online flank, angry. He was too moderate, too sympathetic to Israel, too accommodating to lead Democrats in the House, they argued. Four others joined the recalcitrant in voting against his nomination.
 Jeffries pushed back, not with words, but with votes: 251 of them. If he gets the same tally on the House floor in January, it will be only the second time since the 1994 “Republican Revolution” that a candidate for speaker has eclipsed 250 votes and the first time since retiring Rep. Nancy Pelosi , D-Calif., picked up 255 votes in 2009. Either way, he will make history as the first Black speaker of the House. 
 The “Stubborn Seven” — Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York; Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania; Adam Hamawy of New Jersey; Melat Kiros of Colorado; Donavan McKinney of Michigan; and Frederick Haynes of Texas — cast what some lawmakers call “hero” votes. That is, they decided to risk retribution from party leaders, and ostracism by their peers, in order to flex muscle for a national constituency of the far left. All but Hamawy and Haynes are members of the Democratic Socialists of America.
 The seven wrote in a statement that they have “worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations” on issues including “Medicare for All” and ending the war in the Gaza Strip. 
 “While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership,” they continued. “Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no.”
 But if they were seeking to create leverage, their gambit backfired. Archimedes purportedly said that if given a place to stand and a lever, he could move the world. By taking their stand, these seven Democrats risk kneecapping themselves with the lever.
 Now, it’s clear that Jeffries doesn’t need their votes. He could lose 33 more and still win the speaker’s gavel next year. He may never need them for anything. Perhaps he will choose to be magnanimous and refrain from punishing them. But he may also not go out of his way to help them. It is the speaker who decides which House members can use public funds for congressional delegation trips abroad. It is the speaker who controls the internal panel that picks committee assignments. 
 As one former House Democratic chief of staff said in an interview today, Jeffries could decide to resurrect a long-since-disbanded backwater panel — the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service — and stock it with the seven freshmen who voted against him.
 Then again, they may have inadvertently done Jeffries a favor: They showed the rest of their caucus, and the party’s voters, just how strong of a position he will be in at the start of his speakership.

 Trump’s legal fight against congressional investigations could outlast his presidency
 By Lawrence Hurley
 When Democrats issued subpoenas in 2019 seeking information about President Donald Trump ’s finances, it prompted a furious legal fight that wasn’t resolved until after he left office at the end of his first term.

 Slide 1 of 1 The House Oversight and Reform Committee ended up getting some of the information it sought from the accounting firm Mazars in 2022, during the Biden administration, but by then the political value of it had receded.
 The same happened with attempts by Democrats to obtain Trump’s tax records, which were finally disclosed in late 2022 after the Supreme Court declined to intervene .
 With Democrats now about to take control of Congress and vowing to launch a new wave of investigations on issues ranging from the Trump family businesses to immigration enforcement, history could repeat itself.
 The Trump administration has already pledged to fight requests for information, even launching its own threats to prosecute members of Congress for mounting unwarranted investigations, despite legal immunity lawmakers have under the Constitution.
 “If you delay enough, people move on to the next outrage,” said Emily Berman , an expert on executive power at the University of Houston Law Center.

 🗞️ Today's other top stories
 🇨🇳 Summit setup: In a rare and surprising move, Chinese President Xi Jinping personally greeted President Donald Trump as he arrived in China. Trump will hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin tomorrow, in addition to their trilateral meeting with Xi. In an interview with NBC News , Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Trump and Xi could apply enough pressure on Putin to end the war in Ukraine if they wanted to. 
 ☑️ Final Senate call: Former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska , NBC News projects, a victory that will give Democrats a 56-44 majority in the Senate next year. Read more → 
 💊 Over(ton) and out: The White House has dropped Dr. Heidi Overton ’s nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration amid concerns from Republican senators over her experience. Read more → 
 ✈️ Not so fast: The Trump administration’s request for $50 billion in new Federal Aviation Administration funding after a nationwide ground stop strangled air travel is running into skepticism from both parties on Capitol Hill. Read more →
